title: Secondary socialisation
lead: Secondary socialisation is the continuing learning that happens outside the home, through agents such as education, peers, the media and religious organisations.

p: Secondary socialisation is the continuing process of learning norms, values and roles beyond the earliest learning in the family. Agents include education, peers, media and workplaces.
In plain words, it is what you learn about wider society once you are out in the world beyond your family.
In Parsons’ three stages, secondary socialisation comes second. The child learns what wider society expects of its members, and this generally takes place outside the home.

Parsons’ third stage is tertiary socialisation. This is adult socialisation and takes place when people need to adapt to new situations such as becoming a parent, changing jobs, coping with illness or death. Some textbooks call the workplace a secondary agent; your course treats adult socialisation as a third stage, tertiary socialisation.
list: Who: agents outside the family, such as friendship groups, education, mass media and religious organisations.
When: after primary socialisation, for example when children start school, meet new people and develop peer groups.
How: by learning the norms, values and roles that each agent expects, including the hidden curriculum at school, such as punctuality and respect for authority.

p: A school teaches pupils to be on time and to respect authority, which are part of the hidden curriculum.

Media can convey messages about the behaviour and roles expected of boys and girls, and other agents can challenge those messages. A girls’ football team, for example, may challenge the idea that sport is mainly for boys.

writers.name: Parsons
writers.says: Described three stages of socialisation. Secondary is the second stage: the child learns what wider society expects of its members, mostly outside the home.

writers.name: Giddens (2006)
writers.says: Said that socialisation is the process through which humans learn and internalise their culture’s norms and values, which is passed from generation to generation.

p: Here are three ways secondary socialisation can look in 2026.
list: A sixth-form student learns how sixth form works, including free periods, private study and the expectation that students manage their own time.
A group chat teaches what is acceptable to post and how quickly people are expected to reply, because friends react when someone breaks the unwritten rules.
Joining a school football team teaches a pupil the roles of captain, player and substitute, and what each one is expected to do.
